contracted power target raised to 5 GW; >1 GW/yr new build from 2027; connected power 800MW-1GW held

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

Capacity and footprint: total manufacturing capacity on track to exceed 6,000 racks per month, including MORE THAN 3,000 DIRECT-LIQUID-COOLING racks per month, with most DLC rack production lines supporting the densest 250kW rack platforms. Announced a new 32-ACRE DCBBS campus in Silicon Valley featuring an advanced optical-photonics networking lab and datacenter-scale manufacturing, bringing the U.S. footprint to nearly 4 million square feet; Taiwan, Malaysia and the NETHERLANDS facilities are also ramping strongly.
>6,000 racks/mo incl >3,000 DLC racks/mo at 250kW; 32-acre SV DCBBS campus

Power and cooling readiness at the CUSTOMER site was the direct cause of the Q4 revenue shortfall - short-term customer delays in power, cooling and networking pushed revenue out of Q4 into subsequent quarters. DCBBS is the response: a turnkey stack of DLC solutions, CDU, chill door, water tower, power shelves/battery backup, 1.6T high-speed switching and networking, Supermicro Data Center Management software (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM Orchestration Manager) and full lifecycle services, plus a new PROACTIVE SERVICE model going online early next quarter where management software and field teams auto-alert and pre-stage repairs to stop compute capacity loss. DCBBS was previously guided to ~20% of gross profit and management says '20% should be not far away'. Liquid cooling penetration keeps rising - GPU and CPU platforms alike (Vera, Rubin) are liquid-cooling-ready and management expects liquid cooling to dominate the datacenter business soon.
Q4 miss from customer power/cooling readiness; DCBBS ~20% of gross profit target

Q2 GAAP EPS $1.42 and ADJUSTED OPERATING EPS $2.55, up $0.64 YoY, driven by Calpine accretion, HIGHER PJM CAPACITY PRICES and commercial-book performance (realized customer margins + portfolio optimization through volatility), partly offset by more planned nuclear refueling outage days and Illinois ZEC revenue timing ($85M of banked credits recognized vs $200M a year ago - a timing item already inside guidance; the Illinois ZEC program ENDS IN MAY 2027 and this was the final planning-year true-up). FULL-YEAR 2026 ADJUSTED OPERATING EPS GUIDANCE RAISED $0.50 TO $11.50-$12.50 (from $11-$12) at the halfway mark - 'our midpoint is now what used to be the top end of the guide' - with the outlook to be revisited on the Q3 call after summer
Q2 adj EPS $2.55 (+$0.64 YoY); FY26 guide raised to $11.50-12.50

LONG-TERM NUCLEAR CONTRACTING RESTARTED: ~920 MW of long-term nuclear deals signed since the last call, at an AVERAGE DURATION OF 18.5 YEARS, all with INVESTMENT-GRADE customers, priced 'consistent with our view of long-term value' (the $20-$50/MWh disclosure range from March is retained, and management confirmed the executed PPAs fit inside it). Roughly 30% OF CLEAN BASELOAD OUTPUT IS NOW UNDER LONG-TERM AGREEMENT, with the pipeline called 'robust and active'. Counterparties are not disclosed at customer request; the one named deal is WALMART - Walmart's FIRST nuclear PPA and the first such transaction by a major retailer. Critically, management confirmed these are signed contracts that are NOT dependent on the outcome of the pending FERC/PJM decisions. Because the new agreements have later start dates they are not expected to materially affect 2029 earnings, but they extend visibility on base-earnings growth
~920 MW signed, avg 18.5-yr term; ~30% of clean baseload now contracted

CRANE (Three Mile Island) RESTART ON TRACK FOR 2H 2027: the NRC approved the new-fuel licensing amendment request, clearing the path to receive new fuel, and FERC granted the waiver to TRANSFER CAPACITY INJECTION RIGHTS FROM THE EDDYSTONE facility (slated to close) TO CRANE - expected to clear many of the transmission contingencies identified in PJM's initial deliverability review so Crane can deliver full value to the grid. Fleet life extension continued with subsequent license renewal applications filed for GINNA and NINE MILE POINT 1, enabled by New York's extension of the ZEC program, leaving 'the vast majority of our power generation secured through 2050 and beyond'. Operations: 93% nuclear capacity factor and 40 TWh generated while completing SIX refueling outages (capacity factor down 1.8pts YoY purely on planned outage days); 23-day average outage duration - 40% better than the industry average - including a turbine upgrade at Byron Unit 1; nuclear capacity factor ran ABOVE 99% during the Mid-Atlantic heat wave before July 4
Crane restart 2H 2027 (NRC fuel amendment + Eddystone capacity rights); 93% CF, 40 TWh

REGULATORY UNLOCK FOR LARGE LOADS moving far faster than expected. FERC in June ordered EVERY RTO to justify (or revise) how its tariff provides just and reasonable interconnection of LARGE LOADS, and directed PJM to explain why co-located transmission services cannot be made available more quickly; FERC is also willing to study GENERATION AND LOAD TOGETHER AT A COMMON POINT OF INTERCONNECTION, which Constellation has advocated. PJM released proposals for the RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT (RBP) and INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE (IRAS), set a target of 6.8 GW for the RBP, and is running a BILATERAL MATCHMAKING process to pair customers with new supply and shrink the centrally procured amount; the RBP auction is proposed for this fall with RESULTS BY YEAR-END. Co-location rule clarity is now expected in Q1-Q2 2027 (PJM response due ~November 2026, FERC order Q1-Q2 2027) versus PJM's earlier 2029 target. Separately Constellation is urging the EPA to exclude FERC-tariff-directed curtailments from the 50-HOUR ANNUAL LIMIT on data-center BACKUP GENERATORS, which management says may be the most effective way to cover the few peak hours
PJM RBP target 6.8 GW, auction this fall; co-location clarity Q1-Q2 2027 (was 2029)

THE STRANDED-CAPACITY THESIS, restated as the core commercial argument: the grid has unused generation and wires capacity in OVER 99% OF THE HOURS of the year - 'we have a peak capacity concern, not an energy concern' - so the fastest and cheapest path to powering AI is harvesting that latent capacity and managing the handful of peak hours with batteries, demand response, peaking resources and customer backup generation. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want. Customer sophistication about the grid is now 'as good as the energy companies themselves' - not true two years ago. Management expects the data economy to invest 'upwards of $1 trillion in infrastructure ANNUALLY' and expects PJM deal flow to 'kick off with a bit of a bang' once rules are final
grid unused >99% of hours; data economy capex 'upwards of $1T annually'

CAPITAL ALLOCATION AND PORTFOLIO: ~$2.2B of accretive share repurchases in the four months since the March outlook (just under $2B since the Q1 call plus the $335M previously disclosed), with $2.8B of authorization remaining. Agreed to sell the BRAZOS VALLEY ENERGY CENTER to LS Power for $860M (~$1,420/kW), satisfying the FINAL DOJ requirement from the Calpine acquisition; total DOJ-mandated divestitures should yield ~$5.9B gross at nearly $1,200/kW, a healthy premium to the ~$960/kW implied purchase price of the Calpine assets - a mark management reads as validation of the acquired gas fleet 'in a soft ERCOT market'. The 2029 capital-allocation sensitivity was updated to a FLOOR of $0.20/share with upside of MORE THAN $0.75/share (previously $0.50+ with no floor). The nuclear PTC 2030 strike price rises from $49.88 to $50.88/MWh on the IRS 2025 inflation adjustment (2.8%), adding ~$0.30/share to the 2030 base-earnings view and supporting the goal of double-digit base earnings growth into the 2030s
$2.2B buybacks YTD ($2.8B left); Brazos Valley $860M (~$1,420/kW); PTC 2030 strike $50.88/MWh

Q3 FY2026 (Apr-Jun) revenue $650M, +8% YoY, but ~$90M BELOW the plan given on the Q2 call — the shortfall was production delays at two new contract-manufacturing facilities that are ramping. Implied Q4 gross margin ~11%.
Q3 revenue $650M (+8% YoY, ~$90M below plan); ~$15M ramp/new-product cost + $15M battery-agreement loss; GM range 10-15% intact (~12% ex one-timers)

FY2026 guidance CUT: revenue to $2.9-3.1B (midpoint $3.0B, ~-$400M vs the prior midpoint) and adjusted EBITDA to -$30M to +$10M (midpoint -$10M vs prior +$50M). Liquidity $863M (incl. $365M cash), expected back to ~$900M by fiscal year-end; management flagged that supporting record order intake may require an ADDITIONAL $300-500M of working capital over the coming year.

Backlog $6.4B record (+14% QoQ, >30% YoY); Q3 orders $1.44B (~3x YoY); YTD orders $2.7B (+80%); pipeline $33.1B; FY27 coverage $2.2B

FIRST data-center revenue: orders and awards totaling $850M. (1) A $300M order for a BEHIND-THE-METER project with a data-center developer — Fluence's first data-center deal — where the developer was referred by one of the two hyperscalers Fluence holds MSAs with and is building that data center for the same hyperscaler; lead-to-order took under three months vs the ~12-18 month cycle in its traditional utility/IPP segment. (2) ~$550M of awards in July across MULTIPLE data-center sites under one of the two hyperscaler MSAs — awards, not yet purchase orders, with final technical points being closed and conversion to backlog expected in the coming months. Data-center pipeline grew to 16 GWh, +35% QoQ, now a mix of hyperscalers (majority) and developers (fastest-growing). Hyperscalers buy on QUALITY of power (load smoothing, low-voltage ride-through via Fluence's operating system); developers buy on SPEED-TO-POWER. All data-center projects are 2-hour duration; margins in line with the rest of the book. Manufacturing delays do NOT touch the MSAs — they affect legacy contracts signed 12-18 months ago.

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

Pipeline stands at an ALL-TIME HIGH with the highest-ever monthly funnel intake in July and a record rolling-12-month funnel; ~3,000 new customers added year-to-date worth >$100M of incremental business; largest customers up high double digits for the year; Southeast Asia more than doubled and is the fastest-growing region. No pull-ins or panic buying detected - management specifically looked for and did not find demand pulled forward by possible sovereign transceiver restrictions.
Record orders $2.091B (+56%); wireline orders MORE THAN DOUBLED; B2B >1.1 two quarters

SUPPLY, NOT DEMAND, IS THE LIMITER. Demand for Keysight's differentiated AI products is 'far exceeding our ability to supply at this point'. The supply environment is 'less flexible today than a year ago'. The constraint has MOVED: three months ago it was internal channel capacity around ramping MIPI on unprecedented early demand (largely fixed); it is now INCOMING PARTS, with numerous players competing for the same component suppliers. Management expects supply to be 'nonlinear' and 'a governor of our ability to convert demand into revenue for the next several quarters', and a governor of near-term FY2027 revenue. Mitigations underway with a lag: an 18-month+ supply-chain planning horizon, REDESIGNING SOME PRODUCTS AT THE MARGIN TO ACCOMMODATE SECOND SOURCES, and longer-term agreements. Q4 guidance is unchanged in confidence despite this.
Demand far exceeds ability to supply; incoming parts now the constraint, nonlinear for several quarters

Company-wide, SUPPLY rather than demand is the limiter: orders $2.091B (+56%, second straight quarter above $2B) against revenue $1.846B (+36%), book-to-bill above 1.1 for two consecutive quarters and backlog built in the quarter. The supply environment is 'less flexible today than a year ago'; the binding constraint has moved from internal channel capacity to INCOMING PARTS, with numerous players competing for the same component suppliers. Management expects supply to be 'nonlinear' and 'a governor of our ability to convert demand into revenue for the next several quarters'. Mitigations carry a lag: an 18-month+ supply-chain planning horizon, redesigning some products at the margin to accommodate SECOND SOURCES, and longer-term supply agreements.
Orders $2.091B vs rev $1.846B; B2B >1.1 two quarters; incoming parts the constraint

Component supply remains tight: demand for certain components is higher than available supply and the supply chain team is working to mitigate it, though Fabrinet has continued to get its share of what it needs. Management declined to name specific parts, citing three-way customer/supplier relationships on high-profile components, and confirmed that any potential supply gaps are already factored into the Q1 guidance and growth expectations for all three revenue categories.

On the proposed U.S. ban on new Chinese transceivers: not a done deal and early days, but Fabrinet does not manufacture for any Chinese providers and is focused on Western providers, so in theory it should be a positive - as long as materials and components are available. Grady cautioned that a large share of transceivers going into data centers today come from China, so an outright ban would bring the whole industry to a halt.

Orders (DART half-year report filed 08-14-2026, as of 2026-06-30): H1 2026 NEW ORDERS KRW 422,483M (1.34x H1 revenue of KRW 314,502M); ORDER BACKLOG KRW 556,788M — up from KRW 477,377M at 2026-03-31 (+16.6% in one quarter) and equal to ~3.4 quarters of Q2 revenue. CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION (anonymised, >=10% of H1 sales): A 32.1% (KRW 100,809M), B 19.9% (KRW 62,606M), C 19.0% (KRW 59,712M), D 18.5% (KRW 58,029M) — top four = 89.5% of revenue; a year earlier the same four were KRW 57,943M / 13,491M / 57,587M / 36,879M, so customer B grew 4.6x YoY. Sales channel: mostly direct to 'top-tier global inverter makers and US utilities'; overseas sales team I covers US inverter/renewables/petrochemical/EPC accounts, overseas sales team II covers overseas utilities and Japanese inverter/reactor makers.
H1 new orders KRW 422.5B (1.34x rev); backlog KRW 556.8B at 06-30-2026 (+16.6% QoQ); top-4 customers 89.5% of sales

Capacity & capex (DART half-year report filed 08-14-2026): 2026 production capacity 44,133 units at the Ansan plants vs 35,431 in 2025 (+24.6%) and 33,368 in 2024; H1 2026 utilisation 87.2% (286,471 of 328,536 available hours); H1 production output KRW 277,943M. Plant #2 (11,000 pyeong, ~2x plant #1's 6,000) has been renovated and is in production; the ongoing KRW 42,000M capex programme (KRW 12,000M plant #2 overhaul/plant #1 repair + KRW 30,000M transformer production-line expansion and automation at both plants, Jan-Dec 2026) is 57.3% spent (KRW 24,043M), with KRW 8,584M due in 2026 and KRW 9,373M from 2027. US STRATEGY: 2025 US revenue ~KRW 380.4B of KRW 501.9B total, yet <2% share of a ~KRW 10T US distribution-transformer market (global ~KRW 40T) — the company plans a US entity for direct sales, a US A/S centre, and 'in the long term a production base in the US'. 2026 capacity 44,133 units (+24.6% YoY); utilisation 87.2%; KRW 42B capex 57% done by 06-30-2026; US entity + A/S centre planned, US production base long-term

Customers announced 10+ new fab projects just this quarter; leading-edge logic and DRAM fabs running at FULL capacity. Largest customers giving rolling 8-quarter forecasts, longer-lead-time POs with cancellation/expedite charges, and some conversations extending to 2030; clean room availability is what governs industry shipments. Applied hiring to have capacity to DOUBLE quarterly system output from current levels by 2028 (+1,500 manufacturing/AGS hires this quarter; new Singapore manufacturing center officially opened; next expansion planned for 2030). Record operating cash flow >$3B, FCF $2.3B.
10+ new fab projects; 2x output capacity by 2028

MEMORY COST PASS-THROUGH AND SUPPLY POSTURE: price increases contributed about FIVE POINTS of top-line revenue growth in Q4, with roughly four to five points planned for FY2027 (weighted to the first half as prior increases lap). Increases are SINGLE DIGIT, applied to HARDWARE ONLY (not software) and targeted at products with higher memory content. Cisco's exposure is structurally lower than server vendors': memory is roughly 15-20% of its bill of materials versus about two-thirds for server-heavy vendors, since ~95% of what Cisco sells is not a server. Internally, more than 30 programs target memory-utilization efficiency — Wi-Fi 7 memory utilization was cut 50% within about 90 days. Management describes price increases as 'a last resort', with customers accepting them as an industry rather than a Cisco issue. On supply: no significant lead-time issues, strategic agreements and advance purchase commitments in place, strategic inventory being built, an equity investment in Nanya on the memory side, and direct dealing with TSMC (no middleman) across wafer, substrates, assembly and test.
price increases = ~5pts of Q4 growth, ~4-5pts planned FY27; memory only 15-20% of Cisco BOM; Wi-Fi 7 memory use cut 50%

→ TSMC: CFO Mark Patterson on securing supply: 'We do not have any middleman between us and TSMC, so when we are securing silicon, we are looking at the whole supply chain, whether it is wafer substrates, assembly, and test, and really dealing directly with TSMC.' Cisco reports no significant lead-time issues 'unlike we have heard a number of different peers talk about', and says it has adequate supply to meet the FY2027 guide and upside beyond it. Cisco plans to roll out Silicon One comprehensively across its high-performance networking systems by FY2029, giving it greater control over the supply chain and innovation pipeline.

Record Q4 revenue $2.05B (+42% YoY pro forma) with data center revenue +66% YoY; FY2026 revenue $7.12B (+28% pro forma) and non-GAAP EPS $5.61 (+59%). Coherent targets its first quarter above $3B of revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. Bookings hit another record: fiscal 2027 is basically completely booked out, backlog runs through the end of calendar 2027, customers are now placing orders into calendar 2028, and LTAs extend through the end of the decade with take-or-pay minimum demand guarantees. Both 800G and 1.6T grow through calendar 2026; indium phosphide capacity remains the primary supply constraint, doubling YoY by the end of the September quarter.
Q4 $2.05B, DC +66% YoY; FY27 booked out, orders into CY2028, LTAs to end of decade

800G is NOT rolling over as 1.6T ramps — Coherent expects 800G revenue to CONTINUE GROWING YEAR-OVER-YEAR through calendar 2026 alongside the rapid 1.6T ramp. Q4 data center revenue +24% QoQ and +66% YoY. Indium phosphide is the binding constraint across the portfolio (assembly and test capacity is available); June-quarter InP laser output — the lasers that feed both 800G and 1.6T transceivers — was up about 80% YoY, and internal InP capacity doubles YoY by the end of the September quarter, one quarter ahead of plan.
800G still growing YoY through CY2026; InP laser output +80% YoY; InP is the constraint

Both transceiver tiers grow together: 800G revenue continues rising year-over-year through calendar 2026 while 1.6T ramps rapidly into 2027 as adoption broadens. Q4 data center revenue +24% QoQ, +66% YoY, the third consecutive quarter of double-digit sequential growth. Supply, not demand, is the limiter — indium phosphide capacity is the primary constraint (assembly and test have headroom), with internal InP output doubling YoY by the end of the September quarter and more than doubling again by end of calendar 2027.
800G + 1.6T both growing; DC revenue +66% YoY; InP the primary constraint

INDIUM PHOSPHIDE IS THE PRIMARY CONSTRAINT on the whole business — 'we're not constrained in assembly and test capacity right now... we're really just constrained by the ramp of the indium phosphide production.' Internal InP output capacity doubles YoY by the end of the current quarter, ONE QUARTER AHEAD of the original plan, and is on track to MORE THAN DOUBLE AGAIN by the end of calendar 2027; substrates and other critical inputs for that ramp are already secured, and capacity beyond 2027 is being planned. Concrete measure: Coherent produced about 80% MORE indium phosphide lasers in the June quarter than a year earlier — those lasers feed 800G and 1.6T transceiver shipments in the current quarter, so management expects data-center revenue growth this quarter to EXCEED 80% YoY. Six-inch lines in TEXAS and SWEDEN are producing EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes with yields that exceed the 3-inch lines across all three device types; a third 6-inch location in ZURICH starts in the first half of calendar 2027. Six-inch economics: 4x the output per wafer at half the cost.
InP output 2x YoY (a quarter early), 2x again by end-CY2027; June-qtr lasers +80% YoY; 6-inch = 4x output at half the cost

Visibility and balance sheet. Record bookings again in Q4: FISCAL 2027 IS BASICALLY COMPLETELY BOOKED OUT and backlog runs through the end of CALENDAR 2027, with customers now placing purchase orders into CALENDAR 2028; customer LTAs extend THROUGH THE END OF THE DECADE and generally carry increasing supply each year, pricing commitments, and minimum demand guarantees (take-or-pay). 'We continue to see no signs of attenuation in customer demand.' Q4 capex $556M (versus $290M in Q3 and $131M a year earlier) and expected to rise sequentially again in Q1; data-center investments carry a roughly 18-MONTH PAYBACK and the capacity is fungible across product lines. FY2026 debt payments $513M, ending leverage 0.7x versus 2x at the end of FY2025; year-end cash $2.59B (from $3.05B in Q3 and $1.63B at end FY2025). Gross margin has risen in EIGHT OF THE PAST NINE QUARTERS for a cumulative +660bps; the Investor Day target is >42% (Q1 guide midpoint 40.5%) and management says it will raise the target once reached. Opex is already below the 18% target model at the Q1 guide midpoint.
FY27 booked out, orders into CY2028, LTAs to end of decade; Q4 capex $556M, ~18-mo payback; leverage 0.7x

Q2 2026: group revenue $582M (+454% YoY, +46% QoQ); the Nebius AI business grew faster at $575M (+514%), 98% of group revenue. Annualized run-rate revenue reached $3.0B at end-June (+598% YoY, +56% from $1.9B at end-March). Group adjusted EBITDA $236M (versus a $21M LOSS a year ago and $129.5M last quarter) at a 41% margin, up from 32% in Q1; the Nebius AI business alone did $286M of adjusted EBITDA at a 50% MARGIN, with the group/AI gap reflecting early-stage investments in Avride and TripleTen. Growth drivers: capacity added in Q1, higher utilization from infrastructure efficiency, plus high-margin revenue from the new asset-light model, Token Factory and recent acquisitions. 'Once again, we sold out of capacity because as fast as we bring capacity online, we can sell it.' FY2026 guidance REAFFIRMED across all metrics: ARR $7-9B, group revenue $3-3.4B, group adjusted EBITDA margin ~40%, capex $20-25B.
rev $582M (+454%); ARR $3.0B; group adj EBITDA 41%, Nebius AI 50%; FY26 guide reaffirmed

FIRST CAPACITY AUCTION as a price-discovery mechanism: it cleared at the highest price Nebius has ever seen for the BLACKWELL generation — 15% ABOVE THE HIGHEST PRICE IT HAD EVER CHARGED and 20% ABOVE its Blackwell pipeline pricing. Management framed it as letting the market set price directly in an environment where 'competitor pricing, analyst opinions, and even prediction markets are all over the place' and 'we have several buyers for every GPU'; the winning bidder plans to participate in future rounds. Both the auction and the short-term scale-training deals remain take-or-pay, use only a small portion of total capacity, and have faster close-to-deployment cycles. On competitive entry (xAI selling compute at premium prices), CEO Arkady Volozh said new entrants 'validate the market' — the AI cloud market is growing tens of gigawatts per year while Nebius plans roughly 1 GW per year, so hyperscalers 'cannot build all of it'.
first auction cleared 15% above highest price ever charged, 20% above Blackwell pipeline

Confirmed from the customer side: Lumentum signed an indium phosphide substrate supply deal with AXT during its fiscal Q4 (quarter ended 06-27-2026). Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston said a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand 'across a couple of customers' forced Lumentum to spend the last three months securing more substrate supply - 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner. Wupen has worked with them for a good number of years.' Lumentum says it is comfortable near-term on its lead Japanese supplier arrangement plus AXT, but that this 'may not be true a quarter or two from now' if the demand vector continues.
AXT deal signed in Lumentum fiscal Q4; driven by ultra-high-power laser demand surge

→ Lumentum: Lumentum confirmed the AXT indium phosphide substrate deal from the buyer side, signed during its fiscal Q4 (quarter ended 06-27-2026). Trigger was a surge in ultra-high-power (CPO/NPO) laser demand across a couple of customers that outran Lumentum's existing substrate arrangements: 'we have seen a pretty big surge in demand... in order to respond to that, we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT.' Lumentum expects it may need still more substrate supply if the demand vector continues.

Supply-demand imbalance update: no change on EMLs (still shipping behind customer demand, previously cited at greater than 30%), but high-powered lasers have deteriorated sharply - 'we are way behind in our shipments... The demand signal has increased, and we are very much further behind relative to our ability to supply.' Management clarified the ramp execution itself is on track; the gap widened because demand accelerated. High-powered lasers were named as the one vector that materially changed since the prior quarter.
EML imbalance unchanged (>30%); high-power laser shortfall materially worse on accelerating demand

Pump lasers: shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year and Lumentum will 'remain effectively sold out for the foreseeable future despite our rapid capacity expansion.' A fourfold increase in pump laser shipments is still expected over the next several quarters. Share is roughly 70%-80%. Capacity is ramping at Rose Orchard (US) with packaging and test in Thailand. Multiple long-term customer agreements have been secured to help offset planned capital expenditures - mostly three-year arrangements with built-in pricing levers and, in most instances, take-or-pay structures, formed largely with NEMs (network equipment manufacturers).
pump lasers +80% YoY; 4x shipment increase expected; ~70-80% share; 3-year take-or-pay LTAs

InP substrate supply: after a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand across a couple of customers, Lumentum spent the last three months securing additional substrate supply and signed a deal with AXT during the quarter. Hurlston: 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner.' Lumentum is comfortable near-term on the strength of its lead arrangement with a Japanese supplier plus the AXT deal, but flagged that given the rate of change in the demand vector 'that may not be true a quarter or two from now either' - more substrate help is likely needed if the vector continues.
AXT InP substrate deal signed in Q4; more substrate supply likely needed if demand vector continues

Balance sheet / working capital: completed $5.6B of equity offerings in Q4 ($1.4B common stock + $4.2B mandatory convertible preferred), cash $7.5B, borrowings + converts $8.7B, net debt cut to $1.2B from $7.5B; no plan to use the ATM program. Q4 operating cash flow +$747M and free cash flow $722M on $28M capex (FY2026 operating cash flow -$6.8B, capex $162M). Closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built ahead of higher FY2027 revenue; cash conversion cycle 149 days (from 106) - DIO 119, DSO 59, DPO 29 - expected to normalize on the tighter contract terms written into the current backlog. Inventory/generation-transition risk managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems reusable across product lines and generations.
$5.6B raise; net debt $1.2B; inventory $12.9B; CCC 149 days

Component procurement scaled ahead of the FY2027 ramp: closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built in anticipation of higher revenue; the $5.6B June equity raise is described as fully supporting component supply and business needs. Generation-transition risk on memory and other components is managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems that stay compatible across product lines and generations - with management noting that with prices rising so fast, older inventory has often been resold favorably.

Record demand and de-concentrating customer base: over $60B of NEW ORDERS booked in Q4 FY2026 (~70% pure AI, ~30% CPU / CPU-based AI / edge AI), taking order book and backlog to record levels entering FY2027. NINE customers exceeded $1B of revenue in FY2026 versus four in FY2025, and the largest datacenter/CSP customer was 28% of FY2026 revenue. The $1B+ cohort is described as a lot of emerging Neoclouds and CSPs plus some enterprise customers. FY2027 revenue guided to $65-72B.
$60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

MEMORY SHORTAGE SPILLOVER INTO OPTICS: 100G revenue will DECLINE in Q3 because one customer cannot source enough 100G SWITCHES to meet its forecast - management attributes the switch shortage to the MEMORY SHORTAGE and expects 100G weakness to persist 'until the memory supply recovers' (CEO: back to normal 'within a few months, either by end of this year or next year'). Quantified impact: ~$20-25M of lost 100G single-mode transceiver revenue in Q3; without it Q3 growth would be >50% Q/Q instead of ~35-45%.
-$20M to -$25M of Q3 100G revenue lost to the memory-driven switch shortage

CPO / ELSFP EXTERNAL LASER SOURCE ECONOMICS: ELSFP (external light source for co-packaged optics) is in very limited production now, ramping later in 2026 and through 2027 to ~400,000 PIECES PER MONTH IN 2028. Laser power scaling is the constraint: CPO/ELSFP uses a 300mW laser vs 70mW in an 800G transceiver and 100mW in a 1.6T transceiver, with die size ~6x larger, so meeting CPO demand requires the industry laser market to be 8-10x BIGGER than today; the next generation of ELSFP moves to DWDM, where yield loss is 40-50% worse than 1310nm. Laser capacity carries a 21-24 MONTH equipment-to-high-volume lead time. AOI is engaged with ~5 CPO customers on 3-4 year demand; several have already qualified AOI on fixed-wavelength CPO laser / ELSFP, with DWDM the current focus. High-volume ELSFP manufacturing is 'more like late Q3 next year' (late 2027). Houston laser fab capacity to grow ~300% by Q3 2027 plus a SECOND FAB cleanroom ~4x the size of the current facility (adding MOCVD, epi, steppers). Margin mix: laser gross margin 55-65%, ELSFP module ('EOSAP') >50%, both landing H2 2027. AOI is absent from first-generation CPO deployments purely because laser capacity must first feed AOI's own transceivers.
ELSFP ~400k pcs/month in 2028; 300mW CPO laser vs 70mW(800G)/100mW(1.6T); industry laser capacity needs 8-10x; laser GM 55-65%

BOTTLENECK HAS MOVED FROM LASERS TO DSP/TIA: because AOI makes its own lasers in-house it avoids the laser shortage that management calls 'the biggest bottleneck right now for the transceiver business' and 'the number one issue' for competitors; AOI's binding constraints for 800G/1.6T are instead DSP and TIA supply, where 'the whole supply chain is very tight' for 1.6T - AOI says its supplier ranks it FOURTH priority under a long-term partnership, with calls once or twice a week. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE SUBSTRATE: supply secured into end-2027 and 'incrementally better' than last quarter - not currently a limiter; AOI has just moved to 4-INCH substrate volume manufacturing and buys from 2 European + 2 Japanese + 3 Chinese suppliers, and is negotiating partnerships or a possible JOINT VENTURE with 2-3 of them for 2028-2029 volumes (laser capacity growing 'much more than a factor of 10'). Proprietary in-house production machinery insulates AOI from the industry's equipment-delivery bottlenecks.
DSP/TIA = binding constraint (AOI ranked 4th priority); InP substrate secured to end-2027; 4-inch substrate volume production

Named by AOI management on its Q2 FY2026 call as one of the very few suppliers able to serve the high-power CPO laser market: AOI, Lumentum, Coherent and Broadcom are all 'invest[ing] huge money' in laser capacity, yet 'even combined... it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years'. Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.
Industry high-power laser capacity must grow 8-10x for CPO; 21-24 month equipment lead time

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a fully automated enclosure plant with 15 GWh/year capacity that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that operates its main Vietnam enclosure facility. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (the 'pods' that sit on the skids) failed Fluence's testing and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and the site reached full production in Q4. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.
Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

SOURCING: Fluence signed a long-term battery-cell agreement with an INTERNATIONAL supplier that covers not just supply but technology-roadmap alignment on how cells behave inside Fluence's modules — securing long-term volume and attractive pricing for FY2027-28 and letting it price future orders with more confidence, at the cost of a $15M charge on one in-flight project supplied by the same counterparty. Explicitly NOT related to AESC (the AESC review, run earlier in the year, drove some strategic expense but produced no announcement); Fluence says it is spending a lot of time talking to battery capacity across the market and sees an opportunity to work more closely with U.S. battery manufacturers. On inverters: Fluence uses ONLY non-Chinese inverters in the U.S. — mostly U.S.-made, some imported from Europe — so it expects zero impact from the FCC's inverter restrictions; in Europe it still uses a mix of Chinese and non-Chinese and is working toward a fully European solution ahead of expected European restrictions.
Long-term cell supply + tech-roadmap agreement (int'l supplier, not AESC), $15M charge; 100% non-Chinese inverters in the U.S.

Capacity and balance sheet: NOT capacity constrained - in-house factories support ~$2B of revenue and the Asian EXTENDED FACTORIES have now added essentially an equal amount of capability, with shorter cycle times, second shifts running and third shifts available; the extended-factory model also cut freight and labor cost and lowered capex needs, a large driver of the 2026 margin expansion. Supply chain is called the residual risk, managed by 'leveraging our balance sheet' to build inventory. Nearly $1.9B of cash and short-term investments; $62M operating cash flow (>100% of net income); May completion of a $1.5B 0%-coupon convertible due 2031 (~$1.2B net cash) plus ~$200M of buyback and a capped call struck at $509.06. Analyst day set for December 17 at the NYSE
capacity ~$2B in-house + equal from extended factories; cash ~$1.9B

NEW-BUILD ECONOMICS GAP: ERCOT year-to-date wholesale power has averaged $30/MWh (same as last year) versus the ~$90/MWh area cited for new-build contracting — '30 is not going to get new stuff built.' The price of generation EQUIPMENT 'has doubled, if not tripled' in some cases, so what was an acceptable build price a year or two ago no longer is. In PJM the $555/MW-day RPB cap 'might get some things built' but a spread around it will be needed for certain projects. Large-load customers are willing to contract with EXISTING assets at a PREMIUM because it is still a discount to new build; co-location can beat even an islanded new build on speed.
ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

Market outlook: the NAND market is estimated to EXCEED $300 BILLION in calendar 2026 (up 3x YoY) and to APPROACH $500 BILLION in calendar 2027. Data center's share of total NAND TAM expands from ~30% in CY2025 to ~50% in CY2026 and continues outpacing the market in 2027. Demand from customers is growing faster than Sandisk's supply, so bits are expected to REMAIN ON ALLOCATION BEYOND CALENDAR 2027. Sandisk plans to grow with the market rather than outgrow it, holding segment share.
NAND TAM >$300B CY2026 (3x YoY) -> ~$500B CY2027; DC share 30% -> ~50%; on allocation past CY2027

VISIBILITY EXTENDING TO 2031: having previously disclosed one large-customer LTA running to CY2029, WD is now 'in the throes of discussions' to establish LTAs for CALENDAR 2029, 2030 AND 2031 - volume line of sight is described as good, with the open item being the pricing/commercial construct. Forward exabyte demand growth guided at 25%+ (Q4's +22% framed as mix lumpiness - customers taking more CMR in a given quarter ship fewer bits per unit than UltraSMR-heavy customers - not a demand signal). THE BUYER BASE IS BROADENING BEYOND HYPERSCALERS: neoclouds, FRONTIER AI LABS and sovereigns are now coming directly for supply, and one AUTONOMOUS-VEHICLE customer's CY2027 exabyte demand has increased MULTIPLE-FOLD. Enterprise OEMs are also pivoting BACK TOWARD HYBRID storage after flirting with 100% all-flash arrays, adding further demand. Expanding the Dell AI factory ecosystem with partners including NVIDIA, Google Cloud, OpenAI, SpaceX AI, Mistral, ServiceNow, Palantir, CrowdStrike.
ISG record $29B (+181%); memory the primary supply constraint

Agentic AI is expanding the CPU TAM: 'the agent needs support of a CPU... the harness — the CPU runs it, makes the calls, manages memory, and is in the loop in every decision an agent makes' (all 3 microprocessor leaders cited CPU TAM expansion). Traditional server revenue +92% with absolute unit growth AND content growth. Architecture mix: large direct-liquid-cooled GPU deployments (GB200/B300, Vera) are biased to Arm, while enterprise B200/B300/RTX 6000 Pro systems are x86; traditional servers remain x86 today, with Vera CPU seen as future relief for the microprocessor shortage.
Traditional servers +92%; big GPU racks Arm-biased, enterprise x86

Supply-constraint rank order per Jeff Clarke: DRAM, NAND, CPUs (microprocessors), then hard drives, then 'the basket of goods around that'. Trailing semiconductor nodes are filling at greater rates, leading-edge nodes fully allocated with ~1-year lead times. Dell is 'repricing every day' in the inflationary environment, and customers are signing 3-5 year multiyear supply agreements to secure access. Year-over-year, each server carries MORE cores, MORE DRAM and MORE NAND (content growth on top of unit growth).
Constraint order: DRAM > NAND > CPU > HDD; leading-edge lead times ~1 year

Booked $24.4B of AI orders in Q1 and recognized $16.1B of AI server revenue; exited with record $51.3B AI backlog and a 5-quarter pipeline at MULTIPLES of backlog, growing across Neo Clouds, sovereigns and enterprises individually. AI customer count surpassed 5,000, up over 50% in the last 6 months. Capacity is not the limit — 'it's parts': demand exceeds supply with memory the primary constraint, and Dell expects to exit FY2027 with meaningful backlog.
Q1 AI orders $24.4B; backlog $51.3B; >5,000 AI customers (+50%/6mo)

Indium phosphide substrate shortage, asked directly on the call: "Indium phosphide is a very sought-after commodity these days. We are working closely with our suppliers to mitigate any kind of indium phosphide shortages that we are seeing. Ultimately, the main component here will be to dual source or to increase really our sourcing capabilities and ensuring that we are just not reliant on one supplier alone." IQE is monitoring it jointly with suppliers and customers. On its own epi capacity, by contrast: "Right now, we are not seeing any capacity constraints as mentioned in our revenue outlook" - the existing asset base can support the 2026, 2027 and 2028 demand increase "without significantly increasing our fixed cost base."
InP substrate shortage across the market; IQE dual-sourcing to de-risk. IQE's own epi capacity unconstrained - can absorb 2026-2028 demand without material fixed-cost increase

Capacity conversion is the swing factor for InP epiwafer supply, and it is gated on customer commitment: "We also have the ability to flex assets and convert existing tooling to support indium phosphide growth, but this would need to be tied to concrete customer commitments." On converting GaAs lines to InP: "Our tool set is flexible to some degree. We can certainly transfer or convert capacity from our technology to the next. That kind of conversion would again need to be tied to discrete customer demand and visibility to that, because obviously it does come with downtime of the tools and also CapEx commitments." On Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy: "We are monitoring demand very closely, and as mentioned, we are converting capacities if and when that demand materializes." Additional MOCVD tools would come via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment - "any kind of capacity expansion or addition of tools will need to come with customer commitments." Wafer-diameter transitions (4->6 inch, 6->8 inch) are customer-driven, with no company-wide push.
GaAs->InP tool conversion and Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy, both gated on concrete customer commitments (LTA / co-funding / tool consignment)

→ MACOM: "We have also signed long-term strategic agreements with MACOM, which will provide security, revenue visibility, and stability for IQE, and further strengthens our relationship with a tier 1 well-established customer." The LTAs were signed alongside MACOM's strategic investment, which closed the morning of the call. Asked whether MACOM is the main driver of the >20% FY2026 revenue growth guide: "any kind of LTA agreement does give us visibility and transparency on demand and enables us to truly plan for capacity in the right way. It is a driver of that growth, obviously" - though IQE declined to quantify and stressed it is "working on multiple fronts and not just relying on just one player alone." MACOM COO Robert Dennehy and VP David O'Carroll were nominated as IQE non-executive directors. No standstill agreement prevents MACOM from increasing its stake.
value: GBP 45M investment (GBP 30M cash equity + GBP 15M convertible loan notes) within a GBP 81M fundraise; LTA value not disclosed

MACOM secured upstream epiwafer supply by investing GBP 45 million into IQE (GBP 30 million cash equity plus GBP 15 million of convertible loan notes) as the anchor of IQE's GBP 81 million fundraise, which completed 05-28-2026, and by signing long-term strategic supply agreements with IQE at the same time. IQE describes MACOM as "a tier 1 well-established customer" and says the LTA gives IQE "security, revenue visibility, and stability." MACOM COO Robert Dennehy and VP David O'Carroll were nominated to IQE's board as non-executive directors, subject to customary due diligence. No standstill agreement prevents MACOM from increasing its IQE stake.
GBP 45M invested in IQE (GBP 30M equity + GBP 15M convertible loan notes)

N3 AI accelerator for the #1 North American customer is READY FOR PRODUCTION - shipments begin JUNE 2026; Alchip secured the required capacity across ALL suppliers (wafer, CoWoS, substrate, COOLING, tester) for on-time delivery. Ramp: revenue jumps in June, another jump in Q3, monthly revenue PEAKS from mid-Q3; Q3 and Q4 each significantly above Q2; momentum extends into late 2027 followed by next-gen mass production. End-demand keeps rising (analysts cited the customer recently signing multi-gigawatt deals incl. a 5GW Anthropic deal), but 2026 upside is LIMITED - wafer+CoWoS turnaround is 6-7 months ("order today, chips in December"); upside levers = extra N3 wafers (the scarcest capacity in the industry, hard to get) and YIELD improvement; working closely with the customer to maximize 2027 upside. Wafers are the bottleneck, NOT CoWoS - TSMC commitment to this project is very high; open to non-TSMC 2.5D packaging only on capacity shortage (has done it before); HBM is consigned by the customer, Alchip handles everything else even at the chiplet stage.
N3 MP ships June 2026; monthly peak from mid-Q3; 2026 upside capped by 6-7mo turnaround

Supply chain strategy: shares 5-year demand forecasts with small number of key suppliers; ~$1B supplier prepayments in FY2027 (starting Q2) back forecasts with cash; track record of hitting commitments builds allocation priority; same playbook enabled Marvell to scale revenue during prior supply crunches when broader industry remained constrained

NAND market view: AI INFERENCE servers are driving overall CY2026 NAND demand growth and inquiries are getting even stronger; conventional servers remain solid. NL-HDD replacement is running SLOWER in CY26 than first expected — customers prioritize high-performance inference products (TAM still expanding). Smartphone NAND flat CY25->CY26 (low-end units down on BOM-cost inflation; high-end average capacity rising); PC units down on BOM costs. CY2026 industry bit growth high-10s% — SUPPLY-CONSTRAINED; CY2027 demand expected to EXCEED supply. Kioxia to grow bits at least in line with market.
CY26 bit growth high-10s% (supply-capped); CY27 demand > supply; AI inference the driver

Q1 2026 (DART quarterly report, consolidated): revenue KRW 164.9B (+32.8% YoY; products 79.2% / parts & service 20.8%; domestic 71.2%), operating profit KRW 10.7B, net income KRW 22.1B. FY2025 reference: revenue KRW 909.8B / OP KRW 73.8B. Equipment: PECVD, ALD, diffusion/thermal systems (GEMINI line) for semiconductors plus display etch/laser drill; 59 semiconductor tools produced in Q1. Filing: the HBM SHORTAGE is driving memory makers' aggressive DRAM-centric capex, and 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than a normal cycle recovery.
Q1 rev KRW 164.9B (+32.8%); OP KRW 10.7B; HBM-shortage capex cited as driver

Q1 2026 (DART quarterly report): revenue KRW 99.8B (+27% YoY vs KRW 78.4B), operating profit KRW 47.3B — a 47.4% OPERATING MARGIN (+35% YoY vs KRW 34.9B), net income KRW 40.4B. FY2025 reference: revenue KRW 372.5B / OP KRW 177.0B (47.5% margin). Mix: IC TEST SOCKETS 64.1% of sales (KRW 64.0B, of which exports KRW 59.6B) — consumable sockets for memory & logic package test; LEENO PIN spring-contact probes 24.7%; ultrasound medical parts 10.5%. ~30,000 SKUs, fully vertically integrated, short lead-time custom production.
Q1 rev KRW 99.8B (+27%); OP KRW 47.3B (47.4% margin)

Demand visibility jumped: total book-to-bill 1.34 (semis 1.47, passives 1.23), backlog +21% to $1.6B (5.7 months); customers placing orders on 1-YEAR forecasts and building safety stock in Asia for AI applications; distributors extending lead times especially on AI-related products. AI data-center revenue was <$100M in 2025 and will be 'well above that' in 2026 (AI segment growing ~20%+), helped by supply concerns at competitors — 'it's about quick delivery now'. Price increases (metals-driven) announced Q4'25/Q1'26 add ~1-1.5% to ASPs in Q2, more effective in Q3.
B2B 1.34 / backlog $1.6B; AI rev well above $100M in 2026; ASP +1-1.5% Q2

Products & TAM: Eagle G5 + Hawk (sub-6-micron bump-height metrology, 100nm inspection, high throughput) were 30% of 2025 revenue and expected to DOUBLE in 2026; lead times Eagle ~3mo, Hawk 3-6mo with capacity flexibility for upside. Visual Layer acquisition CLOSED — breakthrough AI detection/metrology/classification being integrated (revenue contribution from H2 2026), plus a planned AI-software product line sellable into the thousands-of-systems installed base; AI features expected to expand 2D share and win NEW process steps INCLUDING FRONT END -> TAM grows ~+$0.5B to OVER $2B in 2027. US chiplet IDM customer: meaningful share, business toward late 2026 into 2027. China: healthy but 2026 growth mainly non-China; only one meaningful local competitor.
Eagle G5+Hawk revenue 2x in 2026; TAM >$2B 2027; Visual Layer AI closed

Supply-demand: total SAP (semi-additive process) substrate demand is expected to EXCEED the industry's supply capacity as IC package substrates get larger and more multi-layered. Ibiden capacity expansion plan: CY2024 = 1.0x -> 1.8x CY2026 -> 2.5x CY2028, focused on cutting-edge AI; management says expanding capacity BEYOND the current plan through fiscal 2028 will be difficult (human-resource and lead-time constraints). Material cost increases are being passed through to customers. Competitive position: at new-generation product launches Ibiden typically takes ~100% share (declining 20-30% after 3-6 months); in silicon-bridge substrates the backside-interconnect difficulty should preserve its technological advantage at least through fiscal 2030.
SAP demand > industry capacity; Ibiden capacity 1.0x->1.8x(CY26)->2.5x(CY28); ~100% share at new-gen launch

Strong 300mm wafer demand from leading-edge DRAM for AI data centers is a core part of SUMCO's outlook; memory makers' supply constraints are so tight they are curbing wafer demand from NON-leading-edge logic customers (memory shortage spillover). Long-term contract prices maintained.
leading-edge DRAM wafer demand strong; memory shortage spillover

Wafer market outlook: semiconductor market sees continued strong AI growth and only gradual recovery elsewhere. 300mm demand strong for leading-edge logic and DRAM in AI data centers with a projected NAND uptick ahead; recovery in non-leading-edge logic is gradual and partly TEMPERED BY MEMORY SHORTAGES (memory supply constraints curb non-leading-edge logic demand). 200mm and smaller lacks momentum, inventory-adjustment progress varies by customer.
AI leading-edge strong vs non-AI gradual; memory shortage caps non-leading-edge logic

US transformer market faces severe supply constraints with lead times extended to ~4 YEARS; a major factor is limited availability of grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) and copper — premium GOES is supplied by only a few producers (Nippon Steel, POSCO, Thyssenkrupp), supporting multi-year demand visibility for transformer-core steel into grid/datacenter expansion.
US transformer lead times ~4 years; GOES scarcity

Q3 FY2026 revenue $144.8M (Bitcoin mining $111.2M + AI cloud services $33.6M) as IREN pivots from mining to AI cloud. Secured power increased to 5 GIGAWATTS (one of the largest AI-infra power portfolios in the world). ARR under contract $3.1B, on track to $3.7B exiting CY2026 across 150,000 GPUs; $2.6B cash at April 30. All operational capacity is fully contracted amid acute industry-wide supply constraints. Targeting 480 MW of AI cloud capacity in 2026, scaling to 1.21 GW in 2027.
rev $144.8M (AI cloud $33.6M); 5 GW secured power; ARR $3.1B -> $3.7B / 150k GPUs

Q2 FY2026 (ended March): revenue EUR 3.812B, Segment Result EUR 653M (17.1% margin); Power & Sensor Systems EUR 1.26B (+8% QoQ, SRM 20.4%, +300bps QoQ) driven by AI power. FY2026 guidance RAISED: revenue now up significantly YoY (was moderate), Segment Result Margin ~20%, adj FCF ~EUR 1.65B. AI POWER ON ALLOCATION — demand strongly exceeds supply; converting capacity from other areas (incl. redeploying Dresden front-end from HV automotive drivetrain to AI data center) and ramping new capacity. Reconfirmed dedicated AI power revenue EUR 1.5B in FY2026 -> EUR 2.5B in FY2027. Reorg to 3 business units (Automotive, Power Systems, Edge Systems) from Q4 FY2026.
AI power rev EUR 1.5B FY26 -> 2.5B FY27; on allocation; FY guide raised

Industry-wide shortages 'across the board — wafers, silicon chips, CPUs, optics, and memory' now seen as a 1-2 YEAR phenomenon, not 1-2 quarters; chip lead times running 52 weeks reliably with reservation needs beyond that. Purchase commitments rose to $8.9B (from $6.8B in Q4), multiyear, mostly chips for new products and AI deployments. Deferred revenue $6.2B (from $5.37B) as AI qualification/acceptance cycles stretched from 2-4 quarters to 6-8 quarters (GPU rack-and-stack + manual cabling takes months). Arista will accept gross-margin pressure to assure supply: 'we do not want to keep GPUs idle because Arista did not supply the network'.
52-week lead times; purchase commitments $8.9B; quals now 6-8 quarters

Strong Q1 2026 enterprise results across data center and campus; #1 in >10GbE high-speed switching. Demand described as the best in the CEO's Arista tenure, but facing industry-wide component shortages — wafers, silicon chips, CPUs, optics, and especially memory — with elevated procurement costs; signing multiyear supply agreements and purchase commitments ($8.9B). Demand is outstripping supply in 2026, with expected gross-margin pressure from paying up to assure supply continuity.
industry-wide component shortages; $8.9B purchase commitments; GM pressure
→ AMD: AMD secured HBM supply from its memory partners amid a tight supply environment to support the Instinct ramp

Trainium2 has ~30% better price-performance than comparable GPUs and is largely SOLD OUT; a consistent majority of Bedrock inference workloads run on Trainium; delivered 4x improvement in Trainium2 token throughput during 2025.
Trainium2 ~30% better price-perf, largely sold out

NAND prices rose sharply ~55-60% sequentially in Q1 as AI drives demand across HBM/DRAM/NAND/HDD (NAND shortage expected to persist through 2026-2027). Scaling its cloud-AI opportunity with the enterprise MonTitan NVMe SSD controller and boot-drive (Ferri) products; SSD-controller revenue +45% YoY on early PCIe 5 ramp (8-channel PCIe 5 leads on performance; new 4-channel DRAMless PCIe 5 for mass market). Gaining share as NAND makers outsource more controllers and shift capacity to high-capacity enterprise/data-center, relying on Silicon Motion for consumer + new automotive/AI-smart-storage. Mobile eMMC/UFS up 30-35% QoQ and >140% YoY on controller-outsourcing share gains.
NAND +55-60% QoQ; MonTitan cloud-AI ramp; SSD controllers +45% YoY

Boot-drive/AI-infrastructure footprint expanding: Q4-2025 began volume boot-drive shipments to 'a leading AI GPU manufacturer' for its DPU; in Q1 qualified the next-generation DPU plus Ethernet and NVLINK switches of that customer's new GPU/CPU platform launching H2 2026 — footprint widens beyond the DPU with 2-4x density per device; also sampling with 'a leading search-engine company' for its TPU architecture. NAND sourcing is a moat: 2026 supply allocations were finalized by flash makers by MID-2025, and Silicon Motion secures NAND from 3 different makers; NAND vendors are retreating from edge/client segments (PC units now seen -10%+ in 2026, smartphones -10%+) to prioritize enterprise/cloud AI — accelerating controller outsourcing share gains.
NVLink-switch/DPU boot drives (H2 2026 platform); 2026 NAND allocations locked mid-2025

Q1 2026: RECORD quarter — revenue, gross margin and operating income all MATERIALLY above prior outlook, revenue growth >100% YoY, record Q1 operating cash flow. Full-year guidance RAISED MATERIALLY (non-GAAP EPS now $1.85-2.25; FY2026 expected best in company history). Manufacturing footprint can deliver 5 GIGAWATTS of product annually — "not order constrained and not capacity constrained": revenue pace decided by how fast customers can deploy. Time-to-power has become "an existential necessity" for AI builders bumping into grid/permits/community bottlenecks.
Record Q1, rev >+100% YoY; FY EPS guide $1.85-2.25; 5GW/yr manufacturing capacity

FY2027 (ending March 2027) guidance: sales 2,580B yen (+3.0%), OP 295B yen (+8.3%, OPM 11.4%), net income 225B yen (+15.0%), dividend 40 yen; FCF drops to ~60B yen because CAPEX jumps to 370B yen (HAMR head equipment, suspension expansion, battery tech) with R&D 310B yen. Device assumptions show the MEMORY-PRICE SHOCK hitting ICT: smartphone production -10% (memory shortage), notebooks -12%, tablets -8% - while AI keeps growing: nearline HDD units +7% (71M->76M) and AI SERVER BOARDS +21% (2.2M->2.6M, newly disclosed metric). Segment guide: passive components +5-8% (AI-server products incl. aluminum electrolytic caps), magnetic application +21-24% (nearline HDD head volumes ~+50%, suspension +22%, incl. orders from a captive maker), energy -3-0% (smartphone battery volumes -7% on the handset decline).
FY2027: sales +3%, OP +8.3%; smartphone -10% on memory prices; AI server boards +21%

Q1 2026 (ended March): beat guidance - GAAP revenue 380.3B yen (+23.2% YoY; non-GAAP 372.3B +20.6%), non-GAAP GM 59.2%, non-GAAP OP 125.4B yen (33.7% margin). Timing business divested (excluded from non-GAAP since Feb; pro-forma GM ~49.1% ex-Timing basis per call). DEMAND EXCEEDS SUPPLY: sell-through beat plan so automotive CHANNEL INVENTORY FELL instead of the planned build; AI data-center AND client-AI both growing strongly. Supply is the bottleneck: the Dec-7 Taiwan earthquake (+aftershocks/blackout) hit foundry partners and wafer supply has not caught up (Q1/Q2 impact, big improvement from Q3), plus an industry TESTER SHORTAGE leaves wafers idle - "execution is the key"; if supply executes, results could beat guidance. Utilization ~55% (+6pts QoQ) on MCU + digital-power wafer input. Q2 guide: revenue midpoint 388B yen (+5.1% QoQ pro forma), GM 47.0% (-2.1pts: 1/3 FX, 2/3 manufacturing costs - summer energy, April pay rises, Golden Week maintenance - plus legacy-power mix), OPM 29.0%.
Q1 beat; supply (wafers+testers) is the bottleneck; Q2 mid 388B yen, GM 47.0%

AI data center: digital power (digital controllers for power management) and MEMORY INTERFACE are the profit drivers - "Gen 5 and beyond we are in a good position" (DDR5 RCD-class). Power coverage is GRID-TO-CORE including 48V, expanding toward the grid; "We already have solutions for 800V - a certain GPU manufacturer's publication covers our solution" (800VDC ecosystem). Strong momentum expected through next year with STEP-FUNCTION growth from Q3; expanding in-house capacity and securing additional capacity with Taiwan foundry partners. Caution: short-term AI-power competition is intensifying - "we should not become complacent" (maintain/raise share). PRICING: with transport costs, supply constraints and RISING MEMORY PRICES (and competitors raising prices), "it would be very difficult for us to not increase price... at some point, by some magnitude, we may have to adjust our price."
800V solutions listed by GPU maker; DDR5 Gen5+ interface strength; price hikes likely

Capex decision: ~94B yen approved in Q1, ~80% for CAPACITY EXPANSION - mostly front-end, primarily for AI DATA CENTER DIGITAL POWER built in-house. Kofu fab converting 8-inch products onto 300mm lines (operational visibility in place; depreciation from ~FY2028); allocation of the ~77B capacity portion: roughly half Kofu, >20% Naka, remainder back-end (package/module, still being finalized). In-house DOI policy ~150 days incl. buffer for supply risk/short lead-time needs; channel build continues for data center (advance shipments ahead of new-product certification).
Capex ~94B yen (80% capacity, Kofu 300mm for AI digital power); DOI 150 days

Automotive & EV positioning: stronger than expected - new-gen R-Car SoC ramping successfully while PREVIOUS-generation R-Car/MCUs keep growing (industry using older generations longer than expected); 28nm MCU steady (China customer volatility). EV mix shift is NOT a tailwind for Renesas vs peers: minimal discrete-power exposure and the German competitor holds higher EV-MCU share for now - relative growth muted. Memory-shortage impact on car production seen as manageable (preemptive measures industry-wide), though other shortages (e.g., PCBs) could also constrain. Altium: ARR growth slowed temporarily (platform-adoption and account-count prioritized; old->new model transition), Renesas 365 now generally available.
R-Car new gen ramping + old gens persist; EV = relative headwind vs Infineon

The 2028 game changer: the biggest GPU vendor's next-generation GPU (2028) disclosed 3D stacking that is FORECAST TO BE HYBRID BONDED - equipment ordered in 2026, installed in 2027, volume production from 2028. BESI raised HB bonder capacity from ~15/month (~180/yr) to 250/YEAR, lead time ~6 months (100nm-accuracy tool), able to satisfy any model from "the big five". Long-term model: EUR 1.5-1.9B revenue in 3-5 years (~2.5-3x current) with the support infrastructure being built now; service revenue (15-16% of sales) to move toward 18-20% as the HB installed base adopts a front-end-style 24/7 support model (~900 defined spare parts, 4-hour availability) - a GROSS-MARGIN TAILWIND. Onshoring: TSMC/Amkor/Micron US advanced-packaging fabs build through 2026-27 with volume production from 2028 - BESI engaged in those programs.
Next-gen GPU 2028 = hybrid bonded (orders 2026); HB capacity to 250/yr; LT model EUR 1.5-1.9B

Electrification orders +44% comparable to a record $6.6B - DATA CENTER ORDERS UP TRIPLE DIGITS (DC order CAGR ~35% 2019-2025; strong Q4 AND Q1; pipeline strong, another strong year expected) while the non-DC 90% of ABB still grew double digit. EL revenue +15%, op EBITA margin record 24.0% (+80bps). DC detail: many projects across hyperscalers AND colocation (US/Europe/Asia), NO elephant orders, most orders carry DOWN PAYMENTS, no over-ordering seen; delivery horizon 12-24+ months. Scope expansion: MEDIUM-VOLTAGE UPS gaining share - ABB claims to be the FIRST AND ONLY MV-UPS provider (moves power protection out of costly white space into MV E-houses, cutting opex and build cost); MV UPS is a key building block of ABB's 800VDC ARCHITECTURE coming "a year or two from now" - NONE of today's orders are 800V yet (all upside ahead). Capacity: ABB says IT is not the bottleneck - GAS TURBINES and LARGE POWER TRANSFORMERS are; Senatobia (Mississippi) Smart Power plant doubled in size vs 3 years ago and new lines are ramping; also scaling via OEM partners building switchgear/system integration on ABB's behalf; deliberately allocating capacity across segments rather than selling everything into DC.
EL orders +44%, DC orders +triple-digit; MV UPS unique; 800VDC architecture in 1-2 yrs (orders not yet booked)

Q1 2026 (highest bookings AND billings in years): group revenue $507.9M (flat QoQ, +32.0% YoY, 3-year high, above consensus); group BOOKINGS $727.0M (+46.0% QoQ, +71.6% YoY - 4-year high); adjusted GM 39.5% (+357bps QoQ); adjusted EPS HK$0.81 (+118.9% QoQ, +189.3% YoY, beat). SEMI segment: rev $274.5M (+12.2% QoQ), bookings $309.6M (+43.2% YoY), book-to-bill 1.13 (3rd straight quarter of improvement), adj GM 46.4% (+594bps QoQ), segment profit +165.9% QoQ. SMT segment: rev $233.5M (+60.7% YoY), RECORD bookings $417.4M (+70% QoQ, +101% YoY) on AI servers, optical transceivers, China EVs - SMT high-flex high-force tools for large-format boards are a leading choice for AI SERVER ASSEMBLY. Q2 guide: $540-600M (midpoint $570M = +12.2% QoQ / +37% YoY, above consensus, SEMI-driven); SMT revenue conversion limited by component-supplier lead times, improving H2. Won the Intel EPIC Supplier Award 2026.
Bookings $727M (4-yr high); SMT record $417.4M; Q2 guide $570M mid (+37% YoY)

Data-center power positioning: competing in application-specific sockets — stage-one high-voltage conversion (800V down to 12V/6V) and stage-two VRM / final VCORE multiphase delivery for GPUs — built on 15 years of GaN investment plus advanced BCD nodes manufactured in Texas ('geopolitically dependable'); ASSP design-ins gaining momentum, expected to kick in H2 2026 and into 2027. Beyond ASSPs, an AI rack carries TENS OF THOUSANDS of general-purpose analog parts across many SKUs — TI claims it can fulfill almost every analog socket, and is winning sockets when competitors hit supply shortages.
800V->12/6V stage-1 + VRM stage-2 sockets; tens of thousands of GP analog parts per rack

Kinsus ABF substrate capacity has SOLD OUT (alongside Unimicron and Nan Ya PCB) on escalating AI chip demand; industry ABF quotes expected +5-10% QoQ from Q2 2026, spot prices +30%+; Taiwanese suppliers making AI-chip ABF expansion the primary 2026 capacity goal.
Kinsus ABF sold out; pricing rising

AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.
Hundreds of IC pinouts per tray; hyperscalers ~10% of revenue direct; chiplet + workload emulation
